questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a given bash command and returns its output.

The working directory persists between commands, but shell state does not. The shell environment is initialized from the user's profile (bash or zsh).

IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user:

 - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
 - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
 - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
 - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
While the Bash tool can do similar things, it’s better to use the built-in tools as they provide a better user experience and make it easier to review tool calls and give permission.

# Instructions
 - If your command will create new directories or files, first use this tool to run `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
 - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes in your command (e.g., cd "path with spaces/file.txt")
 - Try to maintain your current working directory throughout the session by using absolute paths and avoiding usage of `cd`. You may use `cd` if the User explicitly requests it. In particular, never prepend `cd <current-directory>` to a `git` command — `git` already operates on the current working tree, and the compound triggers a permission prompt.
 - You may specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). By default, your command will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
 - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. You do not need to use '&' at the end of the command when using this parameter.
 - For git commands:
  - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
  - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
  - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
 - Avoid unnecessary `sleep` commands:
  - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
  - Use the Monitor tool to stream events from a background process (each stdout line is a notification). For one-shot "wait until done," use Bash with run_in_background instead.
  - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — use `run_in_background`. No sleep needed.
  - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause.
  - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
  - Long leading `sleep` commands are blocked. To poll until a condition is met, use Monitor with an until-loop (e.g. `until <check>; do sleep 2; done`) — you get a notification when the loop exits. Do not chain shorter sleeps to work around the block.
 - When running `find`, search from `.` (or a specific path), not `/` — scanning the full filesystem can exhaust system resources on large trees.
 - When using `find -regex` with alternation, put the longest alternative first. Example: use `'.*\.\(tsx\|ts\)'` not `'.*\.\(ts\|tsx\)'` — the second form silently skips `.tsx` files.


# Committing changes with git

Only create commits when requested by the user. If unclear, ask first. When the user asks you to create a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. The numbered steps below indicate which commands should be batched in parallel.

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config
- NEVER run destructive git commands (push --force, reset --hard, checkout ., restore ., clean -f, branch -D) unless the user explicitly requests these actions. Taking unauthorized destructive actions is unhelpful and can result in lost work, so it's best to ONLY run these commands when given direct instructions 
- NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify, --no-gpg-sign, etc) unless the user explicitly requests it
- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it
- CRITICAL: Always create NEW commits rather than amending, unless the user explicitly requests a git amend. When a pre-commit hook fails, the commit did NOT happen — so --amend would modify the PREVIOUS commit, which may result in destroying work or losing previous changes. Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit
- When staging files, prefer adding specific files by name rather than using "git add -A" or "git add .", which can accidentally include sensitive files (.env, credentials) or large binaries
- NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked, otherwise the user will feel that you are being too proactive

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel, each using the Bash tool:
  - Run a git status command to see all untracked files. IMPORTANT: Never use the -uall flag as it can cause memory issues on large repos.
  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.
2. Analyze all staged changes (both previously staged and newly added) and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (eg. new feature, enhancement to an existing feature, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.). Ensure the message accurately reflects the changes and their purpose (i.e. "add" means a wholly new feature, "update" means an enhancement to an existing feature, "fix" means a bug fix, etc.).
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit with a message, ending with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
   Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.
4. If the commit fails due to pre-commit hook: fix the issue and create a NEW commit

Important notes:
- NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands
- NEVER use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- DO NOT push to the remote repository unless the user explicitly asks you to do so
- IMPORTANT: Never use git commands with the -i flag (like git rebase -i or git add -i) since they require interactive input which is not supported.
- IMPORTANT: Do not use --no-edit with git rebase commands, as the --no-edit flag is not a valid option for git rebase.
- If there are no changes to commit (i.e., no untracked files and no modifications), do not create an empty commit
- In order to ensure good formatting, ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC, a la this example:
<example>
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
   Commit message here.
   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

IMPORTANT: When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps carefully:

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel using the Bash tool, in order to understand the current state of the branch since it diverged from the main branch:
   - Run a git status command to see all untracked files (never use -uall flag)
   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote
   - Run a git log command and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the current branch (from the time it diverged from the base branch)
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting. End the body with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

# Other common operations
- View comments on a Github PR: gh api repos/foo/bar/pulls/123/comments

  - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause.
  - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
  - Long leading `sleep` commands are blocked. To poll until a condition is met, use Monitor with an until-loop (e.g. `until <check>; do sleep 2; done`) — you get a notification when the loop exits. Do not chain shorter sleeps to work around the block.
 - When running `find`, search from `.` (or a specific path), not `/` — scanning the full filesystem can exhaust system resources on large trees.
 - When using `find -regex` with alternation, put the longest alternative first. Example: use `'.*\.\(tsx\|ts\)'` not `'.*\.\(ts\|tsx\)'` — the second form silently skips `.tsx` files.


# Committing changes with git

Only create commits when requested by the user. If unclear, ask first. When the user asks you to create a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. The numbered steps below indicate which commands should be batched in parallel.

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config
- NEVER run destructive git commands (push --force, reset --hard, checkout ., restore ., clean -f, branch -D) unless the user explicitly requests these actions. Taking unauthorized destructive actions is unhelpful and can result in lost work, so it's best to ONLY run these commands when given direct instructions 
- NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify, --no-gpg-sign, etc) unless the user explicitly requests it
- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it
- CRITICAL: Always create NEW commits rather than amending, unless the user explicitly requests a git amend. When a pre-commit hook fails, the commit did NOT happen — so --amend would modify the PREVIOUS commit, which may result in destroying work or losing previous changes. Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit
- When staging files, prefer adding specific files by name rather than using "git add -A" or "git add .", which can accidentally include sensitive files (.env, credentials) or large binaries
- NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked, otherwise the user will feel that you are being too proactive

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel, each using the Bash tool:
  - Run a git status command to see all untracked files. IMPORTANT: Never use the -uall flag as it can cause memory issues on large repos.
  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.
2. Analyze all staged changes (both previously staged and newly added) and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (eg. new feature, enhancement to an existing feature, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.). Ensure the message accurately reflects the changes and their purpose (i.e. "add" means a wholly new feature, "update" means an enhancement to an existing feature, "fix" means a bug fix, etc.).
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit with a message, ending with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
   Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.
4. If the commit fails due to pre-commit hook: fix the issue and create a NEW commit

Important notes:
- NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands
- NEVER use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- DO NOT push to the remote repository unless the user explicitly asks you to do so
- IMPORTANT: Never use git commands with the -i flag (like git rebase -i or git add -i) since they require interactive input which is not supported.
- IMPORTANT: Do not use --no-edit with git rebase commands, as the --no-edit flag is not a valid option for git rebase.
- If there are no changes to commit (i.e., no untracked files and no modifications), do not create an empty commit
- In order to ensure good formatting, ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC, a la this example:
<example>
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
   Commit message here.
   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

IMPORTANT: When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps carefully:

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel using the Bash tool, in order to understand the current state of the branch since it diverged from the main branch:
   - Run a git status command to see all untracked files (never use -uall flag)
   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote
   - Run a git log command and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the current branch (from the time it diverged from the base branch)
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting. End the body with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

# Other common operations
- View comments on a Github PR: gh api repos/foo/bar/pulls/123/comments

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacements in files.

Usage:
- You must use your `Read` tool at least once in the conversation before editing. This tool will error if you attempt an edit without reading the file.
- When editing text from Read tool output, ensure you preserve the exact indentation (tabs/spaces) as it appears AFTER the line number prefix. The line number prefix format is: line number + tab. Everything after that is the actual file content to match. Never include any part of the line number prefix in the old_string or new_string.
- ALWAYS prefer editing existing files in the codebase. NEVER write new files unless explicitly required.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid adding emojis to files unless asked.
- The edit will FAIL if `old_string` is not unique in the file. Either provide a larger string with more surrounding context to make it unique or use `replace_all` to change every instance of `old_string`.
- Use `replace_all` for replacing and renaming strings across the file. This parameter is useful if you want to rename a variable for instance.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

content.text:
Good news: I read the actual current implementation, so this plan is grounded in the real code, not assumptions.

## Does `rb_debug_corrupt_for_test` comply with the frozen-API constraint?

Yes, but the earlier phrasing invited a sloppier version of it. The frozen artifact is specifically `include/rbtree.h` — CLAUDE.md's rule is "NEVER modify `include/rbtree.h`," not "never add anything to `src/rbtree.c` beyond the five required functions." Per the spec (§9), `src/rbtree.c` is "your implementation," entirely ours to shape; nothing restricts what private helpers it contains, only that the public contract in the header stays intact and unedited. So a helper function living in `rbtree.c`, undeclared in `rbtree.h`, doesn't touch the frozen contract at all — it's invisible to anything that only includes the header, which is how the grading harness (and any of our own code outside `rbtree.c`) sees the module.

That said, an *always-compiled*, permanently-exported `rb_debug_corrupt_for_test` sitting in the shipped translation unit is worse than it needs to be: it's a standing backdoor into internal state that exists in every build, including `make asan`/`make memcheck` and whatever the grader links against, for no reason except our own five test cases. That's exactly the kind of unnecessary permanent surface CLAUDE.md's "smallest diff, don't refactor unrelated code" rule pushes back on.

## The better version: conditionally compiled, not just conditionally used

Guard the hooks behind a preprocessor macro (`RBTREE_TEST_HOOKS`) that's defined **only** on the compile line for the `test_rbtree` binary in the Makefile — not for `fuzz`, and (by construction) never for any external build that doesn't know to pass it:

- In `src/rbtree.c`, the hook functions live inside a single `#ifdef RBTREE_TEST_HOOKS` block. When the macro is undefined, that block contributes **zero bytes** to the compiled object — not "small," literally absent.
- In `tests/test_rbtree.c`, matching `extern` prototypes (also guarded by the same macro) declare them for that translation unit only. No changes to `rbtree.h`.
- The Makefile gains one flag on `$(BIN)`'s rule (a new `TEST_CFLAGS = $(CFLAGS) -DRBTREE_TEST_HOOKS` used only there). `make asan`/`make memcheck` inherit it automatically since they reuse the same target.

This is strictly better than the "duplicate the private struct layout inside the test file and poke it with `offsetof`" alternative (my Option B, rejected): that approach requires hand-maintaining a second copy of `struct rb_node`/`struct rbtree` outside `rbtree.c`, and if the real struct ever changes, the shadow copy silently desyncs — mismatched field offsets is real, present-tense undefined behavior, which is precisely the failure mode this whole exercise exists to catch. Keeping the mutation code inside `rbtree.c` means there's exactly one definition of the struct in the program, ever.

## Why each corruption is memory-safe by construction

Every hook only **reassigns existing struct fields** on nodes the tree already owns — no `malloc`, no `free`, no pointer created or destroyed. The live set of allocations (node count, key-copy count) is bit-for-bit identical before and after corruption, so `rb_destroy(t)` afterward walks the same real pointer graph it always would and frees everything exactly once. No restore step is needed; destroy *is* the cleanup, and it works regardless of what color/key/size content we scribbled over, since none of the traversal logic depends on validity.

One thing I want to explicitly verify before writing the invariant-5 test: confirm `rb_destroy`'s free loop walks pointers (the Reach/recursion) rather than trusting `t->size` as a bound. From what NOTES.md/CLAUDE.md describe of the Reach teardown, it should — but I'll check the actual code before relying on it.

## Per-invariant design, using the real check order

I read `rb_validate` (`src/rbtree.c:340-369`): it checks in strict order — 1 (root black) → 2 (no red-red) → 3 (black-height) → 4 (ordering) → 5 (size) — and **returns immediately on the first failure**. That ordering is what lets each test isolate its target invariant cleanly, even when a mutation has a side effect on a later check we never reach:

1. **Invariant 1 (root black).** Fixture: any valid non-empty tree. Corruption: `t->root->color = RED`. Check 1 runs unconditionally first, so this returns `1` regardless of anything else about the tree. Fully isolated by construction.

2. **Invariant 2 (no red-red).** Fixture: a tree with enough nodes that some internal RED node has two BLACK children (guaranteed to exist in any valid tree with real internal structure, by rule 4). Corruption: flip one of those BLACK children to RED. Root is untouched (check 1 still passes), so control reaches check 2 and returns `2`. Side effect: this does perturb that subtree's black-height, which would trip check 3 too — but since check 2 fires first and returns immediately, that collateral effect is never reached or observed. Isolated by check order, not by the mutation itself.

3. **Invariant 3 (black-height).** Fixture: a tree where some non-root BLACK node has a BLACK parent and BLACK (or NIL) children. Corruption: flip that node from BLACK to RED. This is the one case I can make genuinely isolated at the mutation level, not just by check order: root color is untouched (check 1 passes), and because both the node's parent and its own children stay black, no red-red pair is created (check 2 still passes) — only the black count along that one path changes, which is exactly and only what check 3 detects. Returns `3`.

4. **Invariant 4 (ordering).** Fixture: any valid tree with ≥2 nodes. Corruption: swap the `key` pointers between two nodes (not the nodes themselves, not the allocations — just which node's `key` field points at which already-owned string). Colors and structure are untouched, so checks 1–3 all still pass; the in-order walk now sees a key sequence that isn't strictly increasing. Returns `4`. Ownership is preserved: each string is still pointed to by exactly one node, just a different one, so `rb_destroy` still frees each exactly once.

5. **Invariant 5 (size).** Fixture: any valid tree. Corruption: `t->size += 1` (or `-= 1`), touching nothing else. Checks 1–4 all still pass since structure/colors/keys are untouched; the final count comparison fails. Returns `5`. (Pending the destroy-doesn't-trust-size check above.)

Each hook should return a status (found-and-corrupted vs. couldn't-find-the-shape-it-needed) so if a fixture doesn't actually contain the structure a given test assumes (e.g., no red node with two black children at the chosen key set), the test fails loudly at setup rather than silently asserting nothing.

---

Does this approach look right to you? If so, I'll implement and verify them one invariant at a time — starting with invariant 1 (simplest, zero preconditions on tree shape), running `make test`/`make asan`/`make memcheck` after each before moving to the next.

## 10. Adversarial Review M2 - Evening 5

Fresh session : reread the ownership/deletion/allocation-failure
requirements in the spec, NOTES.md, and CLAUDE.md, then adversarially review the current
`rb_delete`/`delete_fixup` implementation from scratch — assume a bug exists and keep hunting.
Named three specific bug families to check for going in: a use-after-free in the two-child
successor splice, a copied key leaked on the overwrite path, and an allocation whose NULL return
goes unchecked. Told explicitly not to fix anything, and to flag closely related
ownership/double-free/dangling-pointer/cleanup-path issues if any turned up.

**Real Finding**
rb_validate negative path coverage

The adversarial review found that every existing rb_validate invocation expects a return value of 0 on an already-valid tree. No test deliberately creates an invariant violation and verifies that rb_validate returns a nonzero.

This means the suite verifies that rb_validate acceps valid trees but not that it rejects invalid ones. Because the fuzzer relies on rb_validate as its source of truth, an undetected defect inside one of the checks could allow both the deterministic suite and fuzzer to pass. 

Verdict: this is indeed a real finding, a test-coverage defect, not evidence that rb_validate itself is currently incorrect.

**False Positive**
 
delete_fixup dereferences sib without an explicit NULL guard, which initially looked unsafe. After tracing the red-black black-height invariant for both initial fixup entry and subsequent climb iterations, sibling connot be NULL at any reachable dereference point in a valid input tree. Therefore the missing guard is not an in contract defect. 

Also cleared, all three of the specifically-named suspects from the prompt, each with its own falsification method rather than a bare "looks fine": the successor-splice UAF (traced the `free_own_payload` flag through to the final `rb_free(n)` — the aliased key/value pointer is freed exactly once, never read after being freed; falsifiable with ASan on a two-children delete), the leaked overwrite key (the overwrite branch never re-copies or reallocates a key at all, only `value` changes, so there's no second allocation to leak; falsifiable with `valgrind --leak-check=full` on a tight insert/insert/destroy repro), and the unchecked malloc (all 3 `rb_malloc` call sites — `rb_create`, the node struct, the key copy — are checked with correct cleanup on failure).

Also worth recording: the `sib`-NULL verdict above didn't come out clean on the first pass. Claude initially hedged the induction proof as needing "a targeted fuzzer/asan hit to fully falsify" despite having just given a complete proof with no actual gap in it. Pushed back directly on why a completed proof would need empirical falsification at all — Claude re-examined its own reasoning, found no gap, and retracted the hedge as unwarranted overcaution rather than defending it. Same "verify structurally, don't just trust the trace" lesson as Episode 2, applied here to second-guessing a *correct* conclusion instead of a wrong one.

**Adversarial Review Note**

Despite deep research, Claude still could not find any confirmed ownership/memory-safety defect in rbtree.c. The real finding is that my validator testing isn't independently validating itself.

Told it to check the CS370-HW1.pdf spec directly against each before treating any of them as real work — not just trust DEVLOG's own narrative.

**Judgment: two of three claimed-open items were not actually required, and I caught it by making Claude go back to the spec instead of trusting the log.** Reading the actual PDF (§8.1's repo layout, §9's testing bar) showed `pool.c`/`fault_alloc.c` aren't part of this assignment's structure at all — that's Assignment 2 material sitting in the repo early, not deferred HW1 work. And climb-to-root is explicitly *not* in §9's minimum required table-driven list; the spec's own division of labor pushes rare configurations to the fuzzer's ≥10^5-op bar, which is already satisfied. Only the `rb_validate` negative-path gap was real, confirmed against §9 ("your tests must exercise all invariants") and §16's grading table. Two invented action items would have cost real time for zero credit had I not asked for the spec cross-check.

**Plan revised under direct questioning**

Claude's first proposal was a single always-compiled `rb_debug_corrupt_for_test` helper added to `src/rbtree.c`. Pushed back: does a permanent, unconditionally-shipped internal-state backdoor actually respect the spirit of "frozen API," and isn't there a conditionally-compiled alternative that adds zero cost to a normal build? Claude revised to hooks guarded by `#ifdef RBTREE_TEST_HOOKS`, compiled in only for the `test_rbtree` binary via a Makefile-only flag — so `fuzz` and any external build of `rbtree.c` (including the grader's) never see the symbols at all, versus a helper that would have existed in every build regardless of who's compiling it.

**Tool-output loop, second occurrence of a known failure**

After implementing all five hooks, `make asan` immediately followed by `make memcheck` reproduced the exact ASan/valgrind instrumentation conflict from the 2026-09-13 M2 session (`ASan runtime does not come first in initial library list`) — make's mtime check treated the ASan-linked binary as up to date and valgrind ran against instrumentation it can't coexist with. content.content:
1	# PROMPTLOG
2	
3	Annotated episodes, mostly from M2 (the `rb_delete` milestone: table-driven tests, the deletion
4	plan, `delete_fixup`, and the fuzzer extension), plus Episode 1, a later documentation-only
5	session asked to reconstruct the M1 reasoning behind the Reach (`rb_destroy`'s non-recursive
6	teardown, commit `10104ca`). Each entry is: what I asked, what came back, and my judgment call —
7	accepted, revised, or rejected, and why. Corresponding commits: `71b55ac`, `7bdf93a`, `f32e9ef`,
8	`8fa9072`, `ddfdbf9`. Episodes 8-9 are the coverage-audit session (8 new `delete_cases[]` rows for
9	Case 4/3a/3b, plus the CLAUDE.md/NOTES.md updates describing them), not yet committed as of
10	writing. Episode 10 is a separate, later adversarial review session (fresh context, no memory of
11	Episodes 2-9) targeting memory-safety and ownership correctness directly, also not yet committed
12	as of writing.
13	
14	---
15	
16	## 1. Why rb_destroy uses the Reach now rather than deferring it (M1, pre-dates the M2 episodes below)
17	
18	**Prompt:** Asked Claude why the project decided to implement the Reach (NOTES.md/CLAUDE.md's
19	name for the non-recursive right-spine `rb_destroy` teardown, spec §10) during M1, rather than
20	leaving it as the ungraded, deferred-to-next-assignment technique the spec describes it as.
21	
22	**What came back:** Claude traced the reasoning to two places. First, NOTES.md itself explicitly
23	invites doing it early: after noting recursion is permitted this assignment but revoked next
24	assignment (lines 64-66, "Recursion is permitted this time... the next assignment revokes it,
25	and Section 10 lets you find out early what the revocation costs"), it says "If you want a head
26	start on next month, implement it now behind a second function and check it against your
27	fuzzer's teardown" (lines 75-76). Second, the M1 commit (`10104ca`, "destroy via the Reach")
28	shows it wasn't bolted on afterward — its message states the Reach was "done now rather than
29	deferred (spec §10), swapped in for the recursive bridge used transiently during development,"
30	meaning a simple recursive `rb_destroy` was used as a scaffold while `rb_insert`/`rb_find`/
31	`rb_foreach`/`rb_validate` were being built, then replaced within that same commit, before
32	`rb_delete` or fixup complexity existed to make the teardown logic harder to validate.
33	
34	**Judgment: accepted as an accurate reconstruction, recorded here for the process record.** No
35	code changed — this was a documentation/history question, not a design decision made in this
36	session. Worth logging anyway because CLAUDE.md's "The Reach (ungraded)" section could otherwise
37	read like an unexplained scope decision; the actual motivation (validate the harder
38	non-recursive teardown early, against the fuzzer's own teardown checks, while the tree was
39	still insert-only and structurally simple, rather than retrofitting it after `rb_delete` landed)
40	is worth having on record given the grading note that "a claim with no matching artifact doesn't
41	count."
42	
43	---
44	
45	## 2. Plan revised — the "red sibling" test cases were mislabeled
46	
47	**Prompt:** Asked Claude to trace, for the deletion plan, exactly how each of the 9
48	table-driven `rb_delete` cases reaches the deletion path its name claims, as part of defending
49	the plan before I'd approve it.
50	
51	**What came back:** Claude hand-simulated `insert_fixup` against the two "black leaf with red
52	sibling" test sequences (`d,b,f,a,c` / `d,f,b,e,g`, from `71b55ac`) and initially concluded they
53	were correct. It then built an instrumented scratch copy of `rbtree.c` (dumping real node
54	colors) to double-check its own hand trace before committing to the claim in the plan — and the
55	compiled output disagreed with the hand simulation: both sequences actually produced a **black**
56	sibling with red nephews (Case 4), not the claimed **red** sibling (Case 5).
57	
58	**Judgment: revised, accepted the correction.** Rather than silently patching the tests, Claude
59	flagged the discrepancy, searched (empirically, same scratch harness) for sequences that
60	actually produce a genuine red sibling, and proposed `c,b,d,f,g,l,n` / `p,n,l,k,c,i,e` as
61	replacements. I approved the swap before any test file was touched — this is the correction
62	committed in the "delete black leaf with red sibling" cases now in `tests/test_rbtree.c`. Worth
63	keeping in mind for future sessions: hand-simulating red-black rotations by eye is exactly the
64	kind of thing that looks right and isn't — verify structurally, don't just trust the trace.
65	
66	---
67	
68	## 3. Adversarial review, finding triaged (and traced back to my own error, not the design)
69	
70	**Prompt:** Before letting Claude write `delete_fixup` (the doubly-black rebalancing loop —
71	NOTES.md's own callout that the mirror is "the half people forget"), I had it get a second
72	opinion: a fresh Plan sub-agent, with no memory of our conversation, reviewing the mirrored
73	loop design and the `(parent, x)`-pair approach (needed because this tree's NIL is `NULL`, so
74	`x` can't carry its own parent pointer) against the actual code and NOTES.md, independently.
75	
76	**What came back:** The sub-agent confirmed the mirror was exact, `sib` provably non-NULL,
77	termination provable, and the `transplant`-then-`delete_fixup` ordering safe — but flagged an
78	apparent invariant-2 violation in the specific example tree I'd fed it for "Trace 2" (a red node
79	`k` with a stated red child `i`).
80	
81	**Judgment: finding triaged, not accepted at face value.** Claude re-checked the flagged trace
82	against the *actual* committed test fixture (`p,n,l,k,c,i,e`, delete `p`) rather than the
83	fixture text in the review prompt, and found the real tree was valid — the invalid-looking
84	example was my own transcription slip when writing the sub-agent's prompt, not a bug in the
85	design or in the committed tests. This is exactly the outcome I wanted from an adversarial
86	review: a finding gets checked against ground truth (the repo), not rubber-stamped either way.
87	
88	---
89	
90	## 4. Tool-output debugging loop — a valgrind run that looked like a real bug, wasn't
91	
92	**Prompt:** After `delete_fixup` was implemented, asked Claude to run the full battery
93	(`make test`, `make asan`, `make memcheck`) to confirm the "done" bar from CLAUDE.md.
94	
95	**What came back:** `make memcheck`, run immediately after `make asan`, printed a suspicious
96	valgrind report — `ASan runtime does not come first in initial library list`, then `0 allocs, 0
97	frees`, `HEAP SUMMARY: in use at exit: 0 bytes in 0 blocks` — and exited nonzero. Read at face
98	value this looks like the program didn't even run.
99	
100	**Judgment: diagnosed correctly, not treated as a real leak/crash.** Claude fed the raw output
101	back into its own reasoning rather than guessing, and traced it to a Makefile timestamp issue:
102	`make asan` had rebuilt `build/test_rbtree` linked against ASan, and `memcheck: all` doesn't
103	force a rebuild when the source files haven't changed, so valgrind was handed an
104	ASan-instrumented binary — which conflicts with valgrind's own instrumentation. Fix was
105	`make clean && make memcheck`, which came back fully green (232/232 and 19,842/19,842
106	allocs/frees across both binaries, 0 valgrind errors). I accepted the diagnosis and the fix
107	without asking for a second pass, since the clean-rebuild result was unambiguous.
108	
109	---
110	
111	## 5. Plan accepted under direct interrogation — no revision needed
112	
113	**Prompt:** Across several turns, pushed on the `rb_delete` pseudocode directly rather than
114	just reading it: asked what happens when the successor is the immediate right child (no
115	intermediate parent), whether two nodes transiently alias the same key/value allocation after
116	the copy step, and what happens when the spliced node is the root itself.
117	
118	**What came back:** Claude traced each scenario concretely against the actual `transplant`
119	logic (not just re-describing the pseudocode), including a worked example using the real
120	`d,b,f,a,c,e,g` fixture for the "no intermediate parent" case, and correctly identified the
121	aliasing window as real-but-harmless (guarded by the `free_own_payload` flag) rather than
122	denying it existed.
123	
124	**Judgment: accepted as-is.** None of these questions surfaced an actual bug — each answer held
125	up, and I approved the pseudocode, the STEP0+1 slice boundary (deferring `delete_fixup` to a
126	separate approval), and the corrected test sequences from Episode 2 in the same round. This is
127	the "argue about it now" step NOTES.md itself calls out as worth doing before the walkthrough,
128	not after.
129	
130	---
131	
132	## 6. Re-audit requested, no discrepancies found — but a real coverage gap named instead of hidden
133	
134	**Prompt:** After `delete_fixup` was implemented and committed, asked Claude to re-check its own
135	work: "double check against the 9 table-driven cases... if there are any discrepancies notify
136	me."
137	
138	**What came back:** Claude didn't just re-run the existing suite (which was already green) — it
139	rebuilt a fresh instrumented scratch copy to independently re-verify that each of the 9 cases
140	exercises the exact path its name claims, and hand-verified that the two genuine `delete_fixup`
141	cases produce exact mirror-image trees (strong evidence against a sign error in the mirror
142	branch). No discrepancies were found this time. It also volunteered a residual gap: none of the
143	9 fixtures exercise a multi-level `delete_fixup` climb or a debt reaching the actual root, since
144	those only show up in trees too deep to hand-construct.
145	
146	**Judgment: accepted the "no discrepancies" result, and accepted deferring the named gap to the
147	fuzzer** rather than asking for a 10th hand-built table case — the fuzzer extension (Episode 7)
148	was already the more appropriate tool for that specific gap, and NOTES.md's own note ("We
149	decided to extend the fuzzer to include case 3, where we need an extended fixup to climb up the
150	tree") confirms this was the intended path, not a shortcut.
151	
152	---
153	
154	## 7. Fuzzer extension — approved cleanly, explained for the walkthrough first
155	
156	**Prompt:** Asked Claude to plan the `tests/fuzz.c` extension to cover `rb_delete`, and
157	explicitly asked it to explain the *existing* fuzzer's mechanism well enough that I could
158	present it in a walkthrough myself, not just describe the diff.
159	
160	**What came back:** A plan that first explained the current file's structure in in walkthrough
161	terms (the reference-model-as-oracle design, why the model is deliberately dumb/linear, the
162	per-op branch and periodic `rb_validate`), then the minimal extension (`model_delete`, widening
163	the op choice to 3-way, mirroring the delete contract's two directions) as a small addition to
164	that existing pattern rather than a rewrite.
165	
166	**Judgment: accepted without revision.** The explanation was accurate against the actual file
167	(checked against `tests/fuzz.c` directly, not just the plan's own claims), and the resulting
168	diff (`ddfdbf9`) is exactly what was planned — one new function, a widened branch, one new
169	delete branch, one changed print string. Ran clean under `make test`/`asan`/`memcheck`, plus
170	five extra 200k-op runs at different seeds with no failures, before committing.
171	
172	---
173	
174	## 8. Plan revised twice under direct interrogation — imprecise control-flow claims caught before any test was written
175	
176	**Prompt:** Asked Claude to plan a coverage audit of `delete_fixup` (M2 already landed the fixup
177	itself in commits `f32e9ef` and `8fa9072` — the loop, all cases plus mirrors, on 2026-09-13;
178	tonight's task was closing the gap NOTES.md already names: none of the 9
179	table-driven cases pin Case 4 (sibling black, red nephew) or Case 3 (sibling black, both nephews
180	black) in isolation, or a multi-level Case 3b climb / climb-to-root). Claude proposed a 5-slice
181	plan mapping each spec case to code and tests. Before approving, pushed on four specific claims
182	in that plan rather than accepting the slice boundaries as given.
183	
184	**What came back, and what was wrong:**
185	- Claude's Slice 1 writeup said the Case-5 (red sibling) rotation causes the fixup "loop to
186	  re-enter." Asked for the actual control flow. Claude traced it and admitted the phrasing was
187	  imprecise: there is no `continue` or jump back to `while` after the Case-5 rotation — execution
188	  falls through, in the *same* iteration, into the Case-3/4 check now evaluated against the new
189	  (guaranteed-black) sibling. The loop only actually re-enters if that fall-through lands in
190	  Case 3b (parent black, debt climbs) and sets `x = parent`.
191	- Claude's Slice 2 lumped "sibling black, red nephew" into one case ("Case 4, terminal"). Asked
192	  whether near-red/far-black and far-red-directly are actually the same code path. They aren't:
193	  `rbtree.c`'s `else` branch has an inner `if (is_black(sib->right))` that only fires (and only
194	  then executes `rotate_right(t, sib)` to convert near-red into far-red) when the far nephew is
195	  black; the far-red-direct case skips that block entirely. Two distinct paths through the same
196	  branch, not one — Claude agreed and split Slice 2 into four sub-cases (2a/2b far-red-direct +
197	  mirror, 2c/2d near-red-conversion + mirror) instead of two.
198	- Asked why the plan asserted "no changes needed" for slices that already had passing tests, when
199	  passing tests (plus 10^5-op fuzz + asan/memcheck) aren't the same claim as "this specific named
200	  branch is deterministically pinned." Claude conceded the phrasing overclaimed and restated the
201	  actual scope: the algorithm's correctness evidence is the existing fuzz/asan/memcheck record,
202	  but the fuzzer's *aggregate* pass doesn't identify which named branch fired on any given op, so a
203	  regression isolated to one branch (e.g. the `rotate_right(t, sib)` conversion in Case 4)
204	  could hide behind an otherwise-green fuzz run for a while. Tonight's work makes that
205	  explicit and per-case, not a claim that the algorithm was newly proven correct.
206	- Asked, for Case 3a specifically, to point at the exact line where the red parent gets painted
207	  black — is it inside the both-nephews-black branch, or elsewhere? Claude traced it: the
208	  both-nephews-black branch (`rbtree.c:198-201`) only recolors the sibling and reassigns
209	  `x = parent; parent = x->parent`. The actual recolor happens because the *next* `while`
210	  condition check finds `is_black(x)` false (x is the old red parent), so the loop exits, and the
211	  post-loop catch-all `if (x != NULL) x->color = BLACK;` (`rbtree.c:243`) is what paints it black
212	  — not an explicit `if (is_red(parent))` inside Case 3 itself.
213	
214	**Judgment: plan revised, not rejected outright.** All four corrections were accepted and folded
215	into the plan before any test code was written — this is the "one plan you revised" episode for
216	M2's audit work. None of the four changed the verdict that `delete_fixup`'s algorithm itself is
217	unchanged (it was committed 2026-09-13, before this session); what changed was the plan's
218	*description* of that algorithm's control flow and the honesty of its "verified" claims. Working
219	agreement going forward: derive and hand-verify one slice's tree/insertion-sequence at a time,
220	walk through why it actually enters the named case (mirror included) before writing any test
221	code, and don't pre-derive later slices — exactly the mistake Episode 2 (mislabeled red-sibling
222	fixtures) already burned a turn on, this time caught before a fixture was even proposed.
223	
224	---
225	
226	## 9. Slice-by-slice execution of the Episode 8 plan — search-based derivation, and a claim pushed back on before it was written down
227	
228	**Prompt:** Approved the revised plan from Episode 8, then worked it one slice at a time as
229	agreed: for each of Case 4 (direct + conversion sub-cases), Case 3a, and Case 3b, had Claude
230	hand-derive a candidate tree first, explain why it enters that exact branch (mirror included),
231	and only write the test row after independent verification against a real compiled build.
232	
233	**What came back:** The first two slices (Case 4's two sub-cases) were derivable by hand from
234	7-8 node trees, same technique as the earlier red-sibling case. Case 3a broke that pattern:
235	Claude's hand-built 4-7 node candidates never produced the target shape (a non-root red node
236	with two black children), so it wrote an exhaustive-permutation brute-force search against the
237	real `rb_insert` instead of continuing to guess by hand, and reported honestly that zero
238	permutations at n=4-7 worked before n=8 started producing matches. Case 3b's multi-level climb
239	needed the same escalation one step further: an instrumented scratch copy of `delete_fixup`
240	(counters and case-labeled tracing added, `src/rbtree.c` untouched) driving randomized search
241	over insertion orders, then delta-debug shrinking (repeatedly trying to remove one key at a
242	time, keeping the removal only if the 2-climb property survived) down to a 38-node floor for
243	both the left-starting and mirror-starting cases.
244	
245	While searching for Case 3b, Claude also tried to find a genuine **climb-to-root** case and
246	failed across every strategy tried (random trees to 500 nodes, plus a targeted search for
247	leaves with an all-black ancestor chain — the best-case setup). Its first pass at reporting this
248	concluded the gap should simply be "deferred to the fuzzer" without separating *what failed to
249	appear in a bounded search* from *what the invariants actually rule out*. Pushed back before
250	that framing went into any file: asked for the longest verified sequence with a full trace, and
251	for the claim to be split into what's empirically verified, what follows from the RB invariants
252	(nothing forbids an all-black root-to-leaf path — a fully black tree is a legal RBT), and what's
253	genuinely unproven (whether the *insert-only* fixup algorithm specifically can reach that state,
254	which a few thousand random trials out of a search space too large to sample meaningfully
255	doesn't settle either way).
256	
257	**Judgment: pushed back on and revised before being written down anywhere.** Claude redid the
258	writeup with the three claims kept separate rather than collapsing "not found" into "doesn't
259	exist," and confirmed the spec's actual table-driven requirement (NOTES.md's own explicit list)
260	never named a climb-to-root case in the first place — the "extend the fuzzer" resolution is the
261	project's own prior decision (NOTES.md's Confusions section), not something invented tonight to
262	paper over a gap. Given that, and given the honest three-way split, agreed to add the two
263	verified multi-level-climb rows (8 new table rows total across Case 4/3a/3b, 17 rows overall)
264	and leave climb-to-root to the fuzzer's existing coverage rather than sink more search budget
265	into an open question the spec doesn't require closing. `make test`/`asan`/`memcheck` all came
266	back clean on a full rebuild after the additions. This is the episode that best shows the
267	"verify structurally, don't just trust the trace" lesson from Episode 2 generalizing to a new
268	failure mode: don't trust an absence-of-evidence trace either, without saying so explicitly.
269	
270	---
271	
272	## Note on process coverage
273	
274	M2 didn't produce a genuinely **rejected** diff — every proposed change was ultimately approved,
275	sometimes only after Claude caught and revised its own mistake first (Episode 2) rather than me
276	pushing back on something it insisted was right. If a real rejection happens in M3, it belongs
277	here on its own terms rather than retrofitted into this log.
278	
279	## 10. Adversarial Review M2 - Evening 5
280	
281	**The Prompt**
282	
283	Fresh session : reread the ownership/deletion/allocation-failure
284	requirements in the spec, NOTES.md, and CLAUDE.md, then adversarially review the current
285	`rb_delete`/`delete_fixup` implementation from scratch — assume a bug exists and keep hunting.
286	Named three specific bug families to check for going in: a use-after-free in the two-child
287	successor splice, a copied key leaked on the overwrite path, and an allocation whose NULL return
288	goes unchecked. Told explicitly not to fix anything, and to flag closely related
289	ownership/double-free/dangling-pointer/cleanup-path issues if any turned up.
290	
291	**Real Finding**
292	rb_validate negative path coverage
293	
294	The adversarial review found that every existing rb_validate invocation expects a return value of 0 on an already-valid tree. No test deliberately creates an invariant violation and verifies that rb_validate returns a nonzero.
295	
296	This means the suite verifies that rb_validate acceps valid trees but not that it rejects invalid ones. Because the fuzzer relies on rb_validate as its source of truth, an undetected defect inside one of the checks could allow both the deterministic suite and fuzzer to pass. 
297	
298	Verdict: this is indeed a real finding, a test-coverage defect, not evidence that rb_validate itself is currently incorrect.
299	
300	**False Positive**
301	 
302	delete_fixup dereferences sib without an explicit NULL guard, which initially looked unsafe. After tracing the red-black black-height invariant for both initial fixup entry and subsequent climb iterations, sibling connot be NULL at any reachable dereference point in a valid input tree. Therefore the missing guard is not an in contract defect. 
303	
304	Also cleared, all three of the specifically-named suspects from the prompt, each with its own falsification method rather than a bare "looks fine": the successor-splice UAF (traced the `free_own_payload` flag through to the final `rb_free(n)` — the aliased key/value pointer is freed exactly once, never read after being freed; falsifiable with ASan on a two-children delete), the leaked overwrite key (the overwrite branch never re-copies or reallocates a key at all, only `value` changes, so there's no second allocation to leak; falsifiable with `valgrind --leak-check=full` on a tight insert/insert/destroy repro), and the unchecked malloc (all 3 `rb_malloc` call sites — `rb_create`, the node struct, the key copy — are checked with correct cleanup on failure).
305	
306	Also worth recording: the `sib`-NULL verdict above didn't come out clean on the first pass. Claude initially hedged the induction proof as needing "a targeted fuzzer/asan hit to fully falsify" despite having just given a complete proof with no actual gap in it. Pushed back directly on why a completed proof would need empirical falsification at all — Claude re-examined its own reasoning, found no gap, and retracted the hedge as unwarranted overcaution rather than defending it. Same "verify structurally, don't just trust the trace" lesson as Episode 2, applied here to second-guessing a *correct* conclusion instead of a wrong one.
307	
308	**Adversarial Review Note**
309	
310	Despite deep research, Claude still could not find any confirmed ownership/memory-safety defect in rbtree.c. The real finding is that my validator testing isn't independently validating itself.
311	
312	---
313	
314	## 11. Closing the rb_validate negative-path gap from Episode 10
315	
316	**The Prompt**
317	
318	Asked Claude to compare the M2-era `DEVLOG.md` against the actual repo state and report which
319	open items were genuinely still open. It flagged three: `src/pool.c`/`tests/fault_alloc.c` being
320	empty, the missing `rb_validate` negative-path tests from Episode 10's finding, and the unpinned
321	climb-to-root `delete_fixup` case. Told it to check the CS370-HW1.pdf spec directly against each
322	before treating any of them as real work — not just trust DEVLOG's own narrative.
323	
324	**Judgment: two of three claimed-open items were not actually required, and I caught it by
325	making Claude go back to the spec instead of trusting the log.** Reading the actual PDF (§8.1's
326	repo layout, §9's testing bar) showed `pool.c`/`fault_alloc.c` aren't part of this assignment's
327	structure at all — that's Assignment 2 material sitting in the repo early, not deferred HW1
328	work. And climb-to-root is explicitly *not* in §9's minimum required table-driven list; the
329	spec's own division of labor pushes rare configurations to the fuzzer's ≥10^5-op bar, which is
330	already satisfied. Only the `rb_validate` negative-path gap was real, confirmed against §9 ("your
331	tests must exercise all invariants") and §16's grading table. Two invented action items would
332	have cost real time for zero credit had I not asked for the spec cross-check.
333	
334	**Plan revised under direct questioning**
335	
336	Claude's first proposal was a single always-compiled `rb_debug_corrupt_for_test` helper added to
337	`src/rbtree.c`. Pushed back: does a permanent, unconditionally-shipped internal-state backdoor
338	actually respect the spirit of "frozen API," and isn't there a conditionally-compiled
339	alternative that adds zero cost to a normal build? Claude revised to hooks guarded by
340	`#ifdef RBTREE_TEST_HOOKS`, compiled in only for the `test_rbtree` binary via a Makefile-only
341	flag — so `fuzz` and any external build of `rbtree.c` (including the grader's) never see the
342	symbols at all, versus a helper that would have existed in every build regardless of who's
343	compiling it.
344	
345	**Tool-output loop, second occurrence of a known failure**
346	
347	After implementing all five hooks, `make asan` immediately followed by `make memcheck`
348	reproduced the exact ASan/valgrind instrumentation conflict from the 2026-09-13 M2 session
349	(`ASan runtime does not come first in initial library list`) — make's mtime check treated the
350	ASan-linked binary as up to date and valgrind ran against instrumentation it can't coexist with.
351	Recognized immediately from the prior incident rather than re-debugging it as new;
352	`make clean && make memcheck` resolved it, confirmed clean (547/547 allocs freed for
353	`test_rbtree`, 20,273/20,273 for `fuzz`).
354	
355	**Verification method for the fixtures**
356	
357	Rather than hand-deriving which insertion order would produce a RED node with real BLACK
358	children (invariant 2's fixture) or an isolated BLACK node with a BLACK parent (invariant 3's),
359	compiled a throwaway scratch probe directly against the real, unmodified `rbtree.c` (never a
360	reimplementation — same discipline as the M2 delete-case derivations) to print actual node
361	colors for candidate key sets before writing any test. Confirmed the 7-key fixture's exact shape
362	empirically, then discarded the probe file. All five invariant tests passed with the expected
363	return codes (1-5) on the first run against the real implementation.
364	
365	This closes the last genuinely open *implementation* item from the DEVLOG audit at the top of
366	this episode. What remains after this session is process deliverables only (raw session
367	transcripts, `REFLECTION.md`, and committing this file's own pending edits) — not further code.
